article.headline: Semiconductor Lead Times Are Flashing an Old Buy Signal
article.lede: Among the small set of indicators that chip-sector investors treat as reliable, few are simpler or more durable than the lead-time signal: when the gap between ordering semiconductors and receiving them grows, buy the stocks; when it shrinks, sell. As of spring 2026, that gap is growing across nearly every segment of the industry.
article.body:
The rule is simple enough to fit on a trading card: buy semiconductor stocks when *lead times* are extending, sell when they shrink. Lead times — the gap between placing a chip order and receiving delivery — are the supply chain's most candid expression of demand. When they lengthen, buyers are booking further out because supply cannot keep pace; that scarcity translates to pricing power, margin expansion, and upward revisions to earnings estimates. When they contract, supply has caught up, inventories are building, and estimate cuts follow.

By April 2026, the data supports the buy case. A Baird survey published April 9 found DRAM lead times at **41 weeks** — the highest in the firm's dataset — with *FPGA* lead times at 40 weeks and power-conversion chips from Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR) at 33. The breadth matters: it is one thing for a single hot category to tighten; it is another when analog, power, discrete, and memory all move together. Texas Instruments (TXN) and Analog Devices (ADI) announced 10–30% price increases effective February 2026, followed by ON Semiconductor (ON), STMicroelectronics (STM), and Lattice Semiconductor (LSCC). Price hikes are a lagging but legally enforceable confirmation of what lead-time data signals first. Susquehanna's *SemiSIGnals* tracker — the most closely watched lead-time index among institutional investors — logged five additional days of expansion in Q4 2025.

The tightest segment runs through AI infrastructure. *HBM* — high-bandwidth memory, the stacked DRAM that feeds large AI accelerators — is sold out through at least end-2026, with output at Micron (MU), Samsung (005930.KS), and SK Hynix (000660.KS) redirected overwhelmingly toward AI customers; the three producers have shifted roughly 93% of combined DRAM wafer capacity to HBM, squeezing commodity DRAM supply and pushing spot prices up 80–90% since Q4 2025. NVIDIA (NVDA)'s Blackwell-generation GPU backlog reportedly exceeds $500 billion. *CoWoS* packaging — the advanced chip-stacking process at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) that bonds AI dies and memory — remains oversubscribed through 2026.

The historical precedent behind the maxim is clean. Susquehanna documented lead times climbing from roughly 12 weeks in 2020 to a **peak of 27.1 weeks in May 2022**, coinciding with a sustained bull run in the *Philadelphia Semiconductor Index* (SOX). The unwinding was equally instructive: customers had over-ordered to buffer against the shortage, and when end demand softened, cancellations cascaded upstream — the textbook *bullwhip effect* — driving SOX down more than 30% from its highs and tipping the industry into a deep inventory correction through 2023. The current data suggests the cycle is in early expansion. Whether the second chapter of that script arrives depends on whether AI capital expenditure continues pulling demand outward across every category, or concentrates and eventually plateaus.

concepts.definition: The elapsed time between placing a purchase order for a semiconductor component and receiving physical delivery. Normal lead times run 6–12 weeks for commodity chips. When demand outpaces capacity, that window stretches to 20, 30, or 40+ weeks, forcing buyers to commit capital far in advance — and signaling supply tightness that historically precedes rising prices and stock multiples.

Field-programmable gate array: a chip whose internal logic circuits can be reconfigured by the buyer after manufacture, used in networking gear, aerospace, data centers, and rapid prototyping. Unlike fixed-function chips (ASICs), FPGAs are flexible but expensive. Lead times for FPGAs spike sharply during capacity crunches because production is concentrated among a small number of suppliers.

A monthly lead-time tracking report published by Susquehanna Financial Group that surveys distributors and buyers across thousands of semiconductor part numbers. It is widely treated as the canonical institutional reference for semiconductor cycle positioning, tracking average delivery timelines across analog, memory, logic, discrete, and power categories.

A type of DRAM in which multiple memory dies are stacked vertically and connected via microscopic through-silicon vias, delivering far higher data bandwidth than conventional DRAM at much lower power. It is the memory standard for large AI accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and custom ASICs, and its production is controlled by a handful of Korean and American memory makers.

Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's advanced packaging technology that bonds processor and memory dies side by side on a shared silicon interposer, enabling the tight integration required by AI GPUs. CoWoS capacity is entirely controlled by TSMC, making it a hard constraint on how many AI chips can ship in a given quarter.

The primary benchmark index for US-listed semiconductor equities, maintained by Nasdaq. It includes roughly 30 chip design, manufacturing, and equipment companies and is the standard reference for tracking sector-wide stock performance. Also traded as an ETF under the ticker SOXX.

A supply-chain phenomenon in which small fluctuations in end-consumer demand amplify into large order swings further up the chain. In semiconductors, customers over-order during shortages to secure supply; when end demand softens, they stop ordering entirely, causing cancellations to cascade upstream and production utilization to collapse — often faster and harder than the original shortage.

ticker_mpwr.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
ticker_mpwr.blurb: A fab-light analog company that designs high-density power-management integrated circuits — the chips that step a server's intermediate-bus voltage down to the sub-1-volt rail an AI accelerator actually consumes. MPWR moved from a broad-based analog supplier into the dominant provider of GPU-adjacent power modules during the H100 generation, displacing the incumbent Vicor at Nvidia. Its modules are characterised by very high current density and tight integration, which matter enormously as AI racks push past 100 kilowatts.
ticker_mpwr.recent: In early 2026, management raised the floor on its enterprise-data growth target to 50-percent-plus from a prior 30-to-40 percent range, citing acceleration in Nvidia Blackwell shipments. Analyst notes suggest MPWR may take roughly 70 percent of power-management sockets on the forthcoming Vera Rubin GPU platform (VR200 NVL144 and R200 HGX), potentially adding more than $100 million to 2026 estimates. The stock has gained roughly 90 percent over the trailing twelve months and trades near all-time highs, leaving the AI exposure largely in the price.

ticker_txn.name: Texas Instruments Incorporated
ticker_txn.blurb: The largest pure-play analog-semiconductor maker in the world by revenue, with roughly twenty percent share of the analog market. Texas Instruments designs and manufactures power-management chips, signal-chain devices and embedded processors used in industrial machinery, automobiles and, increasingly, AI servers. Its strategy is unusual in the industry: it owns and operates several 300-millimetre wafer fabs in the United States, giving it a long-term cost advantage against fab-light competitors, but also requiring a multi-year capital-spending programme that compressed free cash flow through 2023-2024.
ticker_txn.recent: Q1 2026 revenue came in at $4.83 billion, ahead of the $4.53 billion consensus, with analog-segment revenue up 22 percent year on year and data-centre revenue up roughly 90 percent. Capital expenditure dropped 40 percent year on year to $676 million as the 300mm fab build-out tapers, and free cash flow rose to $1.40 billion. The company has also announced selective price increases of 15 to 85 percent on certain analog products effective April 2026, in line with similar moves by Analog Devices, Infineon and Murata. The stock is up roughly 50 percent year-to-date through April 2026.

ticker_adi.name: Analog Devices, Inc.
ticker_adi.blurb: Analog Devices is one of the two largest analog semiconductor companies in the world (alongside Texas Instruments), with deep expertise in signal-chain ICs, data converters, and — critical for AI servers — power-management products including hot-swap controllers, multiphase voltage regulators, power-system management ICs (PSMICs), and DC-DC power stages. ADI's LTC4284/4286/4287 hot-swap family protects 48V AI rack infrastructure, while its MAX20790 and related multiphase controllers regulate power to GPUs and accelerators at the point-of-load. The company is also a leading supplier of 800 VDC first-stage conversion solutions designed to NVIDIA's high-voltage DC reference architecture for AI factories.
ticker_adi.recent: ADI reported Q1 FY2026 (quarter ending January 2026) EPS of $2.46 versus the $2.31 consensus, with revenue of $3.16 billion supported by a 50% year-over-year increase in data-centre revenue. AI and data-centre exposure now accounts for roughly one-fifth of total revenues. Q2 FY2026 guidance was set at $3.5 billion (±$100 million), with non-GAAP EPS of $2.88 (±$0.15) and adjusted operating margin of ~47.5%. In August 2025 ADI announced its first 800 VDC hot-swap and first-stage power solutions targeting NVIDIA intelligent platform management, with >98% conversion efficiency. The company has seen accelerating adoption of 48V/54V intermediate-bus converters and smart power stages for vertical power delivery in AI racks.

ticker_on.name: onsemi (ON Semiconductor Corporation)
ticker_on.blurb: onsemi designs and manufactures intelligent power and sensing semiconductors, with a particular focus on silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs and modules under the EliteSiC brand, IGBT power modules, intelligent power modules (IPMs), and gate drivers. The company is a dominant SiC supplier to EV traction inverters and has been rapidly expanding into AI data-centre power delivery, supplying high-efficiency SiC and MOSFET solutions for GPU server power stages. Onsemi claims to be the first vendor to scale vertical GaN production, with 700V and 1,200V devices addressing AI server PSU and rack-level power conversion.
ticker_on.recent: Onsemi reported Q1 2026 revenue of $1.513 billion, above the guidance midpoint, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.64 versus the $0.61 consensus. CEO Hassane El-Khoury stated AI data-centre revenue grew more than 30% sequentially and more than doubled year-over-year in Q1 2026, well ahead of the company's earlier guidance for high-teens growth. Q2 2026 revenue guidance was set at $1.535–$1.635 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $0.65–$0.77. Management reiterated an expectation that AI data-centre revenue will double year-over-year across all of 2026, supported by broader chip-vendor adoption of EliteSiC and new 900V SiC design wins with EV/ESS customers including Geely, NIO, and Sineng Electric.

ticker_stm.name: STMicroelectronics N.V.
ticker_stm.blurb: STMicroelectronics is a global semiconductor group covering microcontrollers, sensors (MEMS), and — most relevant to the AI power-plumbing thesis — a broad power-semiconductor portfolio spanning SiC MOSFETs (STPOWER Gen 4), GaN devices, silicon IGBTs, and power-management ICs. ST is one of only a handful of vendors with an end-to-end 800 VDC power-conversion solution for AI data centres, offering complete reference designs from 800V bus-to-50V, 12V, and 6V conversion using its own SiC and GaN silicon. The company serves automotive, industrial, and, increasingly, hyperscale data-centre customers.
ticker_stm.recent: ST reported Q1 2026 revenue of $3.10 billion, up 23% year-over-year and above consensus of $3.04 billion, with Q2 2026 guidance of ~$3.45 billion. In March 2026 the company announced expanded 800 VDC power-conversion products (12V and 6V architectures) developed to the NVIDIA 800 VDC reference design and showcased at NVIDIA GTC 2026. In February 2026 ST disclosed a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar engagement with Amazon Web Services to supply semiconductors for AWS compute and AI data-centre infrastructure. Management projects data-centre revenue exceeding $500 million in 2026 and surpassing $1 billion in 2027.

ticker_lscc.name: Lattice Semiconductor Corporation
ticker_lscc.blurb: Lattice Semiconductor Corporation develops and sells field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and related development hardware. The company offers small FPGA platforms like Lattice Nexus and Lattice Nexus 2, as well as mid-range platforms such as Lattice Avant. Lattice is a key player in the low-power FPGA market, competing with larger rivals by focusing on edge computing and AI applications.
ticker_lscc.recent: In the past 30 days, Lattice Semiconductor announced a $1.65 billion acquisition of AMI, which led to a stock decline as investors digested the terms. The stock has been volatile, trading near its 52-week high of $127.95, with a market cap of $16.43 billion. Analysts remain bullish with a Strong Buy consensus and a price target of $130.58.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

ticker_005930-ks.blurb: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. is a South Korean multinational electronics company and the world's largest manufacturer of memory chips, smartphones, and consumer electronics. It operates through four divisions: Device eXperience (DX), Device Solutions (DS), SDC, and Harman, covering products from smartphones and TVs to semiconductors and home appliances. As of 2026, it holds a dominant market position in memory and mobile devices, with a market cap exceeding 1,700 trillion KRW.
ticker_005930-ks.recent: In the past 30 days, Samsung Electronics reported strong quarterly earnings driven by blistering memory price hikes, leading to a 46% increase in fair value estimates. The stock hit a 52-week high of 277,000 KRW, reflecting a 390% year-over-year gain. Analysts have raised price targets amid robust demand for AI-related memory chips.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.
